title: Te Hiku Media's te reo Māori speech recognition may be 92% accurate; the University of Auckland tests it on archives, and RNZ begins integrating it into search
summary: Te Hiku Media's te reo Māori speech recognition, trained on 310 hours of community recordings, went from 86% accuracy in its first model to a reported 92% in 2024.
account: Te Hiku Media, a charitable iwi media and technology organization in Kaitaia, New Zealand, built its own te reo Māori automatic speech recognition. MIT Technology Review (22 April 2022) described a ten-day community competition in 2018. It collected “310 hours of speech-text pairs from some 200,000 recordings made by roughly 2,500 people”. From that, bootstrapping an open-source Mozilla model, “Te Hiku created its very first te reo speech recognition model with 86% accuracy”. The tools are offered through the Papa Reo platform. NVIDIA's blog (16 January 2024) says that the model “transcribes te reo Māori with 92% accuracy” using the NeMo toolkit. The University of Auckland announced on 18 March 2024 that its Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound is working with Te Hiku Media. The partners are testing the tool on archival recordings with different dialects, recording qualities and sung forms. Automatic output is compared “against human-generated ones”, with results to be shared with the galleries, libraries, archives and museums sector. The University says that the tool “is performing very well for their purposes” in Te Hiku's broadcasting arm. In September 2024 RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision agreed to supply previously broadcast te reo recordings to train and review the tools. An RNZ release of 11 September 2024 quotes Te Hiku chief executive Peter-Lucas Jones in te reo giving the same 92% figure. The release says that RNZ is integrating the Papa Reo application programming interface into its workflows, first for search and then for captions. No cited source reports a measured outcome for a speaker, learner or archive user. The accuracy figures originate with Te Hiku Media and NVIDIA.
purpose: Te Hiku Media built the tool to transcribe te reo Māori recordings so that learners can search and read archives and broadcasts, under Māori data-sovereignty rules. The transcription tests are that intended use.
system: Te Hiku Media te reo Māori automatic speech recognition and transcription tool (Papa Reo platform; trained with Mozilla DeepSpeech-era open-source tooling, later NVIDIA NeMo)
deployer: Te Hiku Media; test partners Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound (University of Auckland), RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision
taxonomy_note: The documented good is recognition accuracy; serving te reo Maori speakers would be inclusion, but no speaker outcome is reported.

ratings.reason: Te Hiku Media built a te reo Māori transcription capability that it reports at 92% accuracy, up from 86% in its first model. The University of Auckland reports that the tool performs very well in Te Hiku's broadcasting. Both accuracy figures originate with Te Hiku, and NVIDIA, its tooling vendor, repeats the 92% figure.
Benefits to te reo speakers and learners are the stated aim; no cited source measures them.

ai_role.statement: The accuracy figures come from Te Hiku Media. MIT Technology Review reported 86% in 2022. NVIDIA, a tooling vendor, and Te Hiku's chief executive through RNZ stated 92% in 2024. The University of Auckland's independent test compares outputs against human transcripts, with results to follow. No cited source reports an outcome for any speaker, learner or archive beyond the developer's own broadcasting use.

display.answer: The accuracy figures originate with Te Hiku Media. MIT Technology Review reported 86% in 2022. In 2024 NVIDIA, a tooling vendor, and Te Hiku's chief executive, in a release from RNZ, stated 92%. The University of Auckland describes a planned test and the broadcasting arm's use, and it reports no result of the test.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Te Hiku Media's te reo Māori speech recognition, trained on 310 hours of community recordings, went from 86% accuracy in its first model to a reported 92% in 2024.
fields.account: Te Hiku Media, a charitable iwi media and technology organization in Kaitaia, New Zealand, built its own te reo Māori automatic speech recognition. MIT Technology Review (22 April 2022) described a ten-day community competition in 2018. It collected “310 hours of speech-text pairs from some 200,000 recordings made by roughly 2,500 people”. From that, bootstrapping an open-source Mozilla model, “Te Hiku created its very first te reo speech recognition model with 86% accuracy”. The tools are offered through the Papa Reo platform. NVIDIA's blog (16 January 2024) says that the model “transcribes te reo Māori with 92% accuracy” using the NeMo toolkit. The University of Auckland announced on 18 March 2024 that its Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound is working with Te Hiku Media. The partners are testing the tool on archival recordings with different dialects, recording qualities and sung forms. Automatic output is compared “against human-generated ones”, with results to be shared with the galleries, libraries, archives and museums sector. The University says that the tool “is performing very well for their purposes” in Te Hiku's broadcasting arm. In September 2024 RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision agreed to supply previously broadcast te reo recordings to train and review the tools. An RNZ release of 11 September 2024 quotes Te Hiku chief executive Peter-Lucas Jones in te reo giving the same 92% figure. The release says that RNZ is integrating the Papa Reo application programming interface into its workflows, first for search and then for captions. No cited source reports a measured outcome for a speaker, learner or archive user. The accuracy figures originate with Te Hiku Media and NVIDIA.
